interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
A short lesson in twelve small screens. Most show the squared grid and F-shaped flag from Moving the whole plane, with the origin ringed. Arrow i is blue and arrow j is ink, with their names in teal. Two matrix cards sit above the grid, with their product under them. Card A is the shear [1 1; 0 1]. Card B is the quarter turn [0 −1; 1 0].

Play runs the flag through the right-hand card first. A faint ghost stays where that first move left it. Then the flag runs through the left-hand card. The product's columns are where i and j end up. The turn then the shear gives AB = [1 −1; 1 0]. The shear then the turn gives BA = [0 −1; 1 1]. One screen runs AB and BA side by side. Each card there can be set to Turn, Shear, Mirror, Stretch or Do nothing, the identity matrix [1 0; 0 1].

Later screens set the grid aside. A row of the left card lights up beside a column of the right. Their pairs are multiplied and added into one entry of the product. Another screen sets P + Q and 2P beside PQ. The puzzles ask where i or j ends up, which product a run makes, which order the moves go in, and which sizes fit. A wrong pick is drawn, so you can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: The flag slides smoothly from start to finish so you can watch it. A matrix says only where each point ends up, not the path it takes. The grid shows a small patch of the plane, but every point of the plane moves. The picture runs two moves. Three or more chain the same way, with the right-most first.

explain.text:
Do one move of the plane, then another. Together they make a single move with its own matrix. That matrix is the [[matrix product]]. Read AB right to left. B acts first, then A.[^1] It works like f(g(x)). The machine next to x goes first.

One matrix describes the whole run. Each move keeps grid lines straight, parallel and evenly spaced, with the origin fixed. So the two moves together make one move of the same kind. Its columns are where i and j end up. Try it with B as the quarter turn [0 −1; 1 0] and A as the shear [1 1; 0 1]. B turns i to (0, 1). A then pushes that point one square across, to (1, 1). B turns j to (−1, 0). The shear leaves every point on the across axis where it is, so j stays at (−1, 0). So AB = [1 −1; 1 0].

Swap the order and the product usually changes.[^2] In BA the shear acts first. It leaves i at (1, 0) and sends j to (1, 1). The turn then sends those to (0, 1) and (−1, 1). So BA = [0 −1; 1 1], a different move. Some pairs give the same either way. Two turns of the plane do. So does any 2 by 2 matrix paired with the [[identity matrix]] [1 0; 0 1]. That is the do-nothing move.

You can work out the product without drawing. Each entry is a row of A times a column of B. B sends i to B's own column 1. A then moves that point. So column 1 of AB is A times column 1 of B. A times a column gives one number for each row. Each number is a row of A times that column. You multiply matching pairs and add. So the entry in row r, column c of AB is row r of A times column c of B. The top-left entry here is 1 × 0 + 1 × 1 = 1.

Sizes have to fit. A row meets a column pair by pair. So each row of the left must be as long as each column of the right. A 2 by 3 grid times a 3 by 2 grid works. The answer is a 2 by 2 grid.

Adding works entry by entry, but the product does not. Two matrices of the same size add entry by entry. A number times a matrix scales every entry.

**A product of two matrices is one move, the right-hand one first, so swapping the order usually gives a different move.**[^1]

analogy.text: Print a socket-front label on clear acetate and lay it flat on the bench. Give it a quarter turn clockwise, then flip it over left to right. Start again with a fresh label. Flip it first, then give it the same quarter turn clockwise. Follow the outline of the print. One label ends upside down compared with the other. The same two moves in a different order give a different result, just as AB and BA do. Some pairs do match either way. Two turns on the bench give the same result in either order.
analogy.breaks: A real label lifts off the bench as it flips. You can also slide it about. A 2 by 2 matrix keeps the origin where it is, so it cannot slide anything.

practice.text:
- Write the moves right to left. The first move goes on the right.
- For each entry, run along row r of the left and down column c of the right.
- Multiply matching pairs and add. The total goes in row r, column c.
- Check one column. It is where i or j ends up after both moves.

**Rule of thumb:** The right-hand matrix acts first. Rows of the left meet columns of the right.

**Worked example:** Do a quarter turn, then the shear [1 1; 0 1]. The turn acts first, so it goes on the right. That gives [1 1; 0 1][0 −1; 1 0]. Row 1 times column 1 is 1 × 0 + 1 × 1 = 1. Row 1 times column 2 is 1 × (−1) + 1 × 0 = −1. Row 2 times column 1 is 0 × 0 + 1 × 1 = 1. Row 2 times column 2 is 0 × (−1) + 1 × 0 = 0. So the product is [1 −1; 1 0]. Check by following i. The turn sends it to (0, 1). The shear sends that on to (1, 1), which is column 1.

**Sizes:** Each row of the left must be as long as each column of the right. The answer has as many rows as the left and as many columns as the right.

**Counting routes:** A product also counts routes through a network.[^3] Say a and b link to c, d and e, and those link on to f and g. Grid R counts the links from a and b, one row for each. Grid T counts the links from c, d and e, one row for each. Take R = [1 1 0; 0 1 2] and T = [1 0; 1 1; 0 1]. Row b of R times column g of T is 0 × 0 + 1 × 1 + 2 × 1 = 3. So there are 3 routes from b to g, one through d and two through e. In full, RT = [2 1; 1 3].

**Common mistakes**
- Writing the moves in the order you do them. First B, then A, is AB.
- Assuming AB and BA are the same. Usually they are not.
- Multiplying matching entries. That is not the product. Adding goes entry by entry, but the product does not.
- Reading a row of the answer as a landing spot. Landing spots run down the columns.

checks.label: Reading right to left, you first apply the transformation represented by the matrix on the right, then the one on the left: in every run drawn, the flag passes through the right-hand card first, its ghost sits where that card alone sends it, and it ends where the product sends it

Matrix multiplication is not commutative in general: the shear and the quarter turn give one matrix in one order and a different one in the other, and side by side the two flags end in different places

Each entry of a product is a row of the left times a column of the right, pair by pair, added; for every pair of moves and for P and Q this matches running the right-hand matrix and then the left-hand one on every whole point near the origin, and screen 7 works each entry that way

Every worked number is right: AB = [1 −1; 1 0] and BA = [0 −1; 1 1]; B sends i to (0, 1) and j to (−1, 0); after both, i is on (1, 1); the shear sends j to (1, 1) and the turn sends (1, 1) to (−1, 1); MS = [−1 −1; 0 1] sends j to (−1, 1), SM = [−1 1; 0 1]; PQ = [4 8; 6 0], QP = [2 13; 4 2], matching entries give [2 4; 0 0]; P + Q = [3 5; 2 3], 2P = [4 2; 0 6], 2Q + P = [4 9; 4 3]; the top-left of AB is 1 × 0 + 1 × 1 = 1

Sizes have to fit: a product exists only when each row of the left is as long as each column of the right; D (2 by 2) times C (2 by 3) gives a 2 by 3, C times D cannot be worked out, and a 2 by 3 times a 3 by 2 gives a 2 by 2

Some pairs give the same either way: two turns, any card with Do nothing, and the mirror with the stretch; every move keeps the origin fixed, a mirror turns the flag over, and turns and shears keep its size

Each puzzle's answer comes from the rule (B then A for i, the shear first for BA, the first move on the right, rows times columns, doubling then adding, S then M for j, the sizes), and each slip offered is the one its hint names
Each puzzle offers three different answers, accepts only the right one, and draws every wrong one in the warning colour
Before Check, no puzzle shows its answer (no landing spot, no product, no pairing); after a right answer, it does
Every demonstration has finished arriving within its 3 to 4.5 s, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 2.5 s

applied.problem: "the grid is still a grid" fails once i4 shows a zero-determinant move squashing the plane flat; and "two turns" commute only in the plane (3D turns from i6 on do not), and the identity pairing holds for square matrices of matching size.
"two turns" is ambiguous here, since the flip is itself a turn over and does not commute with the quarter turn; only two turns flat on the bench give the same result in either order.
